The Wicked Husbandmen
HUZ-band-men
noun phrase
From the Greek georgos, “husbandman” or “vine-dresser,” the wicked tenants of the Lord’s parable of the rejected Son.

Biblical Definition

The parable of the wicked husbandmen sets forth Israel’s long rejection of the prophets and at last of the Son Himself, and the taking of the kingdom from the unfaithful nation. A householder planted a vineyard, set a hedge about it, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country (Mat 21:33). When the fruit drew near, he sent his servants to receive the fruits, but the husbandmen beat one, killed another, and stoned a third; and so with more servants. Last of all he sent unto them his son, saying, They will reverence my son. But the husbandmen said, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance; and they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him (Mat 21:38; Mat 21:39). The Lord asked what the lord of the vineyard would do, and answered His own question: He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen. The dictionary marks the husbandmen as the rulers of Israel, who slew the prophets and crucified the Son; and the sentence is plain: Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof (Mat 21:43). So the Scripture sets forth Christ as the rejected Son, who is become the head stone of the corner, the LORD’s doing, marvellous in our eyes (Psa 118:22).

Webster 1828 Definition

The Lord’s parable of the tenants who slew the servants and the heir, whose vineyard was taken and given to others.

THE WICKED HUSBANDMEN, the Lord’s parable of the rejected Son.

A householder let out his vineyard and sent for the fruits.

The husbandmen beat, killed, and stoned his servants.

Last he sent his son, and they slew the heir.

The vineyard was taken and given to a nation bringing forth fruit.

Key Scripture

Mat 21:33 — "Hear another parable: There was a certain householder, which planted a vineyard, and hedged it round about, and digged a winepress in it, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country:"

Mat 21:38 — "But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance."

Mat 21:42 — "Jesus saith unto them, Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?"

Mat 21:43 — "Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof."

Modern Corruption

A parable of Scripture; it sets forth the rejected Son, the judgment on the nation, and the kingdom given to a people bringing forth fruit.

expand to see more

The wicked husbandmen have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s parable of the rejected Son and the kingdom taken from the unfaithful. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the guilt of those who slew the heir and the grace that gives the vineyard to a fruitful people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ is the rejected Son who is become the head stone of the corner. The husbandmen, who are the rulers of Israel, slew the prophets and at last the Son Himself, saying, This is the heir; come, let us kill him; and for this the kingdom was taken from the nation and given to a people bringing forth the fruits thereof. So the parable sets forth both the judgment on those who reject the Son and the LORD’s marvellous doing in exalting the stone the builders refused, that He might be the corner of the house of God.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek for “husbandman,” the parable names the wicked tenants who slew the heir and lost the vineyard.

The Wicked Husbandmen — from the Greek georgos, “husbandman” or “vine-dresser.”

A householder let out his vineyard to husbandmen.

They beat and slew the servants he sent for the fruits.

Last they slew his son, the heir.

The vineyard was given to a nation bringing forth fruit.

Usage

"Like the wicked husbandmen, those who reject the Son lose the inheritance they coveted."

"This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance."

"The stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner."
